• Other names: Willow hygro, Willow leaf hygro, Giant hygro
  • Scientific name: Hygrophila corymbosa var. angustifolia / Hygrophila angustifolia
  • Lighting: moderate to high
  • Substrate: nutrient-rich
  • Can be grown emersed: yes
  • Growth rate: fast
  • Placement: background
  • Height: 60–100 cm
  • Fertilizers: optional
  • CO2: optional
  • Propagation: stem cuttings and lateral shoots
  • Colour: green

Studies have shown that Hygrophila angustifolia possesses antimicrobial properties.

Hygrophila angustifolia can be found in tropical and subtropical regions of Asia, including northern and southern Vietnam (Tonkin, Cochinchina), Cambodia, Borneo, China (Yunnan, Sichuan, Hong Kong), Malay Peninsula, Java, Sumatra, Thailand, Indonesia, north-western Australia, New Zealand, New Guinea, and Japan.

It likely originated in the wetlands and rice paddies of mainland Southeast Asia.

This species grows along the banks of streams, rivers, ponds, and rice paddies. It prefers wet soil, still or slow-flowing, and shallow water. It is commonly found in flooded areas, ditches, swamps, and marshes. This allows it to adapt to the periodic changes between rainy and dry seasons.

Due to its significant size and fast growth rate, it is suited only to larger (especially tall) aquariums starting from 80 litres (20 gallons). It also requires space to spread horizontally. Over time it may become so large that you will have to trim and divide it.

• It develops excellently in large and tall aquariums and is easy to care for.
  • Depending on conditions, growth ranges from moderate to very fast. Under optimal conditions the plant can increase its biomass almost 6 times in 30 days.
  • Regular propagation by trimming and replanting stems accelerates growth and creates a dense bush. Pinching stem tips prompts branching.
  • It looks best underwater. Do not allow it to grow above the surface.

Trimming

When the plant is about to touch the surface or lower shoots are aiming to grow taller, it is time to trim. The trimmed parts can be replanted in the substrate, where they readily develop roots.

Trimming long plants can be hard, but it is easy when combined with a water change: lower the water volume, pull the stem, and trim about at water level.

Planting

It suits the background of planted tanks. Remove potted plants gently without damaging roots or stems; remove damaged or decaying parts from cuttings. Bury the roots in the substrate. A stem cutting without roots should have its node completely submerged in the substrate, about 2.5–5 cm deep. Leave enough room between plants: at least 7–10 cm apart rather than one large clump.

If the plant is getting old but is still healthy, gently extract the stem with its roots, find where healthy leaves begin, cut off this part and remove the root portion. If the remaining stem is long, divide it between nodes, making sure each segment has at least three nodes; if short, plant it directly.

Common problems

  • Leggy growth: tall, thin stems with long gaps between leaves, and dropped old leaves. Improve lighting and nutrient balance and prune.
  • White hairs/roots: appear when the plant reaches the surface. Do not let it reach the surface; prune regularly.
  • Overgrowth: it can overrun the tank and shade plants below. Prune and discard the dense mass from time to time.
  • Relocation: it forms massive roots that can uproot a large part of the tank. Remove it slowly, ideally while siphoning the tank.

Temperature: 20–28°C. It does not tolerate cold water; below 20°C it grows slowly.

pH: 6.5–8.0. A slightly alkaline pH is more suitable; too acidic water negatively affects leaves and roots.

Hardness: GH 6–20. Old leaves are much better preserved in hard water (in soft water they decay faster and the plant has to be propagated more often).

Flow: it tolerates moderate water movement, but avoid strong currents.

Lighting: it requires powerful illumination (>40 PAR). Under bright light the pronounced central vein of the leaf acquires a red-brownish colour. Full exposure to light maximizes growth. The photoperiod should be about 12 hours. It tolerates long-term shading, but with insufficient light the leaves become smaller and yellowish, and the stem elongates and becomes leggy.

Substrate: a nutrient-rich substrate at least 5 cm deep is optimal. It is a heavy root feeder, though it also extracts large amounts of nutrients from the water column. It can be kept in sand or gravel with regular root tabs or liquid fertilizers. Some aquarists attach it to driftwood or leave it floating.

CO2: supplementation is optional. It can grow in low-tech tanks, but growth tends to be slower and less bushy. Adding CO2 positively affects growth rate and appearance.

Fertilization: although it has a large root system, it also feeds from the water column. It responds quite favorably to fertilizers.

If you plan to add this plant to a shrimp tank, note that high CO2 levels and copper (contained in most fertilizers) are extremely dangerous to shrimp.

Taxonomy

In the hobby, Hygrophila angustifolia and Hygrophila corymbosa var. angustifolia are often used interchangeably, though some believe they are two different, very similar plants. There are between 46 and 100 species of Hygrophila according to official sources. Care requirements are the same regardless of the exact name.

Etymology

"Hygrophila" derives from Greek "hygro" (moisture) and "philos" (loving), indicating its wetland habitat preference. "Angustifolia" combines Latin "angustus" (narrow) and "folium" (leaf). The name translates to "moisture-loving plant with narrow leaves".

Description

  • A freshwater, erect, perennial, herbaceous plant.
  • Height: typically 60–100 cm and 25–30 cm wide in the aquarium.
  • Stems: hard, square-shaped, up to 5 mm thick.
  • Leaves: narrow and pointed, 2.5–16 cm long and 8–15 mm wide, in pairs, with smooth or slightly wavy margins. Colour ranges from pale green to emerald; the underside is silvery. Under bright light it acquires a red-brownish tint.
  • Flowers: small, in clusters at the joint between leaves and stem; petals usually white with blue or purple markings. They open in the morning and close during the day.
  • Roots: a very powerful root system.
  • It can grow partially or fully emergent. In paludariums (emersed form) it is hardy and needs little care.

The plant shows considerable morphological variability between geographical varieties and environmental conditions.

Propagation

  • Stem cuttings: take 12–15 cm cuttings from the tops of mature stems, cutting between nodes, with at least a few leaves each.
  • Lateral shoots: side branches from the nodes can be cut and planted.
  • Horizontal: lay a stem horizontally and a new stem will emerge from each node. This is one of the fastest ways to increase the number of plants.

Benefits

  • Versatile: grows emersed and submersed, in low- and high-tech tanks.
  • Its root system helps break up anaerobic pockets in the substrate; hydrogen sulfide pockets can be dangerous to fish and shrimp.
  • Fast growth lets it absorb ammonia, nitrates and other harmful substances. In one study, changes after 48 hours were: NH4 2.3–1.6, NO2 0.197–0.152, NO3 1.4–20.1.
  • It helps reduce algae blooms by outcompeting algae for nutrients.
  • It provides cover for small fish, invertebrates, fry and shrimp, and biofilm that is an ideal first food for newly hatched fry and shrimplets.

Quarantine

Unless the plant was grown in vitro and the pot is intact, quarantine and disinfect it before adding it to the tank. Plants may carry parasites, pests such as snails, predators (dragonfly and damselfly nymphs) or pesticide residues that are extremely poisonous to fish, shrimp and other invertebrates.

Without control this plant can become invasive and take over the tank.
